title: VISTA’s infrared view of the Cat’s Paw Nebula
caption: The Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, imaged by ESO's VISTA survey telescope
celestial: Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334 · constellation Scorpius · about 5500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESO/J. Emerson/VISTAAcknowledgment: Cambridge Astronomical Survey Unit

recognition.text: Ranked #35 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This infrared view from VISTA shows the Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, a vast star-forming region about 5500 light-years away in the constellation Scorpius. The whole gas cloud spans about 50 light-years.

Among the nurseries of young massive stars in our galaxy, NGC 6334 is one of the busiest. Some of its stars are nearly ten times the mass of the Sun, and most were born within the last few million years, which is very recent by astronomical standards.

Looking in infrared helps because such young stars are often buried in dust that blocks visible light. Infrared light slips through much more easily, revealing stars and structure that would otherwise stay hidden. VISTA is built to survey wide areas, and this field is about one degree across, which lets the whole sprawling nebula fit in a single frame.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (71.04 x 71.04 arcminutes) and distance (5500 light years), the frame spans roughly 114 × 114 light-years. Its light set out about 5,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from VISTA's VIRCAM camera combines Y, J and Ks filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively.

understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so these colors stand in for wavelengths we cannot see, and dust that looks opaque in visible light becomes more transparent.
